clue.text: One dying to imprison unknown twins, if not for life — criminal

indicators.note: to imprison means one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: an ember is a piece of a fire that is dying out
Z is an algebraic unknown, so twin unknowns give a pair of Zs

indicators.note: if not for life says the little word if is struck out of the word life

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion
the letters removed from life

explanation.surface: A dying convict is spared a life sentence by some strange twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One dying' is the glowing remnant of a fire, not a person; 'if not for life' leaves LE, and 'to imprison' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who embezzles steals money entrusted to them, which makes them a lawbreaker.

clue.text: Uplifting story including chapter for brilliant show

indicators.note: including says the chapter letter sits inside the other piece
in a down clue, uplifting means the word for story is read from the bottom up

parts.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: An inspiring tale with a dazzling chapter makes for a fine performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' turns TALE into ELAT in this down entry, and 'including' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is dazzling success or a striking display of brilliance, a French borrowing.

clue.text: President going topless to screen movie kiss for old video recording?

indicators.note: to screen means to show, here holding the film within
going topless means the first letter of the president's name is removed

parts.note: Barack Obama was a US President
E.T. is the Spielberg film about an alien
X is the conventional written kiss

explanation.surface: A president strips off to show a romantic film scene on an old tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going topless' drops the president's first letter, leaving BAMA; 'to screen' signals the container. The question mark marks Betamax as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Betamax was Sony's videocassette format, now obsolete, so it is an example of old recording technology.

clue.text: Lively metal, not quite grey at the edges

indicators.note: not quite means the final letter of the metal is lost

parts.note: zinc is a metallic element

indicators.note: at the edges means only the first and last letters of grey are used

explanation.surface: A dull metal turns out to be livelier than its greyish rim suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims ZINC to ZIN; 'at the edges' takes G and Y from grey.
explanation.definitionFit: Zingy is an informal adjective for something vibrant, zesty and full of energy.

clue.text: Be like Lear's Pobble, say, sweet thing

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: Edward Lear's nonsense poem is The Pobble Who Has No Toes, so to be like him is to lack toes

explanation.surface: To resemble Edward Lear's toeless Pobble is somehow a sugary matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pobble Who Has No Toes is a nonsense poem by Edward Lear, the Victorian humorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Lactose is the sugar found in milk, so it is literally a sweet substance.

clue.text: Process of renewal with regards to Lance Armstrong's career

parts.note: re is the business-letter word for concerning or with regard to
Lance Armstrong was a professional road racing cyclist

explanation.surface: A comeback story about the disgraced racer's working life.
explanation.definitionFit: Reprocessing waste into reusable material is a way of giving it a new life.

clue.text: Wolves team prepare for trip abroad?

definitions.meaning: a group of wolves hunting together
a rugby team's forwards are its ..., and a group of people can be a ...
before travelling one fills a suitcase with clothes

explanation.surface: The Wolverhampton football side gets ready to fly out for a foreign fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolves is the nickname of Wolverhampton Wanderers, an English football club, which makes the surface about a sports team.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses of one word: a group of wolves, a set of forwards, and filling luggage.

clue.text: Filthy window around top of house, nothing getting wiped

indicators.note: around says the glass word surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a pane is a sheet of window glass

indicators.note: getting wiped means the zero is erased from the roof word

parts.note: the roof is the top of a house
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A grimy window near the top of a house stays dirty because no one cleans it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting wiped' leaves ROF; 'around' signals the container. 'top of house' is the roof itself, not its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Profane language is foul or blasphemous, which is filthy talk in the moral sense.

clue.text: Cold fish on record in sticky wrapper

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
ling is an edible sea fish of the cod family
to film something is to record it, and a film is a record

explanation.surface: Chilled fish sits on a plate wrapped in something clingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Clingfilm is thin plastic sheeting that adheres to itself, used to cover food.

clue.text: Optical illusion ultimately illusory, not sensual

indicators.note: illusory means deceptive, so the letters are not what they seem and must be rearranged
ultimately points to the final letter of illusion

explanation.surface: An optical trick turns out, in the end, to be all in the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives N from illusion; 'illusory' shuffles OPTICAL plus N.
explanation.definitionFit: A platonic relationship is affectionate but without physical or sexual desire.

clue.text: Composer before Liszt sounding note for Sainsbury's?

definitions.text: Composer before Liszt sounding note for Sainsbury's?

parts.words: Composer before Liszt sounding note for Sainsbury's?
parts.note: the Polish composer's name followed by Liszt's is said like the list a shopper takes to a supermarket

explanation.surface: Which composer came just before Liszt?
explanation.walkthrough: Sainsbury's is a British supermarket chain; the two composers' names together are heard as a shopping list.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederic Chopin was a Polish Romantic composer and pianist, a contemporary of Liszt.

clue.text: Look to hold in belly, being short and thick

indicators.note: to hold says the looking word contains the stomach word

parts.note: to spy is to look or catch sight of
tum is a childish word for stomach

explanation.surface: Someone checks their profile while pulling in their stomach to look less squat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hold' signals the container; 'being' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stumpy describes something short and stocky, like the stump of a tree.

clue.text: See 26
An old team with a gas shortage

parts.note: XI is the Roman eleven, a football or cricket team

explanation.surface: An ageing side struggles because there is a lack of fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Anoxia is an absence of oxygen in the body's tissues, a deficiency of that element.

clue.text: Head above dark cloud, perhaps, that requires little thought

indicators.note: in a down clue, above places the head word on top of the other piece

parts.note: nob is slang for the head
a dark cloud is something that rains, a rainer

explanation.surface: A gloomy head in the clouds needs barely any thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above' signals the order in this down entry. A dark cloud is one that brings rain, so whimsically a rainer.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is a decision or task so easy it takes almost no mental effort.

clue.text: Shame meat and beans boiled

indicators.note: boiled means the letters are stewed together and come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A cook is embarrassed by a dish of stewed meat and beans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boiled' rearranges the letters of MEAT and BEANS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is humiliation, the state of being lowered in dignity or esteem.

clue.text: Spreading disease of huge proportions, half caught

indicators.note: caught says the half word is trapped inside the big word

parts.note: epic means vast in scale
demi is a prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: A huge outbreak has infected half the population.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' signals the container; 'half' gives a prefix meaning half, not half of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: An epidemic is a widespread outbreak of an infectious illness in a community.

clue.text: Europeans from Asia, if back to front?

indicators.note: back to front means the front letter is moved to the back

parts.note: Siberians are people from Siberia, the Asian part of Russia

explanation.surface: Are Europeans really from Asia if you turn things round?
explanation.walkthrough: 'if back to front' moves the S of SIBERIANS to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberians are the people of the Iberian peninsula, Spain and Portugal, in Europe.

clue.text: Once more, find European president doing a U-turn

indicators.note: doing a U-turn means the whole run is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: Jimmy Carter was a US president

explanation.surface: Again, discover a European leader reversing his policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doing a U-turn' turns ECARTER round as one run.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrace something is to trace it again, going back over and locating it once more.

clue.text: Vicious people up for a cocktail

parts.note: Sid Vicious was the Sex Pistols' bassist

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for people is read from the bottom

parts.note: a race is a people

explanation.surface: Nasty folk are ready for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid Vicious was a British punk musician. 'up' turns RACE into ECAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidecar is a classic mixed drink of brandy, orange liqueur and lemon juice.

clue.text: Music award lame — about right?

indicators.note: about means the lame word goes around the other letter

parts.note: gammy is British slang for a lame or injured leg

explanation.surface: Is this music prize feeble, or is it fair?
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts GAMMY around R. GAMMY is everyday British slang for a bad leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A Grammy is the American recording industry's annual prize for musical achievement.

clue.text: Team that's sexy not reaching the top, embodying gutless side

indicators.note: embodying means the trimmed word holds the other piece in its body
not reaching the top means the first letter of the sexy word is lost, top being the start of a down entry

parts.note: carnal means sexual or fleshly

indicators.note: gutless means the inside of side is removed, leaving only its ends

explanation.surface: An attractive football side lacks courage on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club. 'not reaching the top' leaves ARNAL; 'gutless' keeps the ends of side; 'embodying' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal is a famous English football club based in north London.

clue.text: Some letters in journalism as the adopted title

indicators.note: Some letters in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of a newspaper's craft is the heading adopted on the front page.
explanation.definitionFit: A masthead is the name of a newspaper printed in large type at the top of its front page.

clue.text: Figure out filling to stop decay

indicators.note: filling means the working-out word fills the stopping word

parts.note: to die is to stop, as an engine dies
to sus, or suss, is British slang for working something out

explanation.surface: Work out which filling will halt tooth decay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' signals the container; SUS is the British spelling variant of suss.
explanation.definitionFit: Disuse is the state of no longer being used, so things fall into neglect and rot.

clue.text: Short, a work for television, perhaps

parts.note: a short is a small measure of spirits, a dram

explanation.surface: A brief piece made for the small screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like an adjective; here it is a noun for a nip of whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama is a play, and a television drama is one such piece made for broadcast.

clue.text: Feature of Cheltenham, perhaps, in the country

parts.note: Cheltenham is a spa town, famous for its mineral springs

explanation.surface: Something characteristic of Cheltenham is found in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheltenham is an English town in Gloucestershire, famous for its spa waters and racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a nation on the Iberian peninsula in south-west Europe.

clue.text: Cuckoo swimming through Paris, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is heard as another word

parts.note: a swimmer passing through Paris would be in the river Seine

explanation.surface: Only a mad person would go swimming across Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The Seine is the river flowing through Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckoo is informal for crazy or mentally unhinged.

clue.text: Succession witnessed cutting hedge technology

parts.note: a chain is a succession of linked things or events
saw is the past tense of see, to witness

explanation.surface: A line of observers watched the latest advances in tools.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition puns on cutting-edge technology: a powered saw is a device for cutting a hedge.
explanation.definitionFit: A motor-driven toothed saw is a tool used to trim trees and hedges.

clue.text: Complimentary, as a run-down battery, say?

definitions.meaning: a flat battery holds no electrical charge at all

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: costing nothing, and having no stored electricity, like a dead cell.

clue.text: Behind time, setter caught in rainstorm finds something waterproof

indicators.note: behind time means the rest follows the time letter
caught in means the setter is trapped inside the shuffled rain letters
storm means the letters of rain are thrown about

parts.note: Paul is the name of this puzzle's setter

explanation.surface: Late, the puzzle-maker gets drenched in a downpour and finds a waterproof cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rainstorm' does double duty: 'storm' shuffles the rain into ARIN, and 'caught in' places the setter inside it. 'Behind time' puts T in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is a heavy waterproof sheet of canvas or plastic used as a cover.
